title: Evaluating a Deterministic Validator Plus Single‑Iteration Repair Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (N=300 paired intent→configuration tasks; preregistration id cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1, preregistration SHA-256 archived) to evaluate whether a minimal guarded pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation (declared model: gpt-5-mini) followed by a frozen deterministic configuration validator and at most one automated repair iteration—reduces first‑pass misconfiguration relative to plain single‑shot generation. Execution completed 600 episodes and used 301 model calls. Observed outcomes: baseline = 299/300 valid (99.667%); guarded = 300/300 valid (100.0%); paired counts n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The single permitted automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). The preregistered planning assumption used for power calculations (planned baseline pass rate = 0.40) was contradicted by the observed near‑ceiling baseline, removing statistical headroom for the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction target. We report preregistered design choices, execution accounting, confirmatory statistics, a post‑hoc inferential sensitivity bound tied to the observed contingency counts, and artifact‑grounded recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory evaluations. All run artifacts and analysis outputs are archived in the execution manifest referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction: Translating high‑level operator intent into device configuration is central to network operations (NetOps). Large language models (LLMs) can synthesize configuration artifacts from natural language intent, promising operator productivity gains. However, probabilistic generation risks misordering, omission, and unsafe commands. Recent literature therefore recommends guarded architectures that pair probabilistic generators with deterministic validators or simulators and bounded repair loops as operational floor‑safety nets. Despite many demonstrations, rigorous preregistered evaluations that quantify how tightly bounded guarded pipelines change first‑pass misconfiguration rates under controlled sampling semantics are limited. We implemented and preregistered a narrowly scoped paired experiment to evaluate a minimal guarded pipeline composed of: (1) a single shared LLM candidate per task (single‑shot generation), (2) a frozen deterministic validator that canonicalizes outputs and applies explicit dependency/workflow checks, and (3) at most one automated repair attempt when violations are reported. Our core research question is: can this minimal guarded pipeline reduce first‑pass misconfiguration rate relative to plain single‑shot generation under a controlled paired design? Contributions: (i) a preregistered paired experiment with deterministic task seeds and archived per‑task artifacts; (ii) confirmatory statistics derived from those artifacts; (iii) a concise post‑hoc sensitivity quantification tied to the observed contingency counts; and (iv) artifact‑grounded recommendations for future confirmatory NetOps evaluations.
sections.related_work: Recent system papers and surveys document progress and limitations of LLMs for intent→configuration synthesis in lab settings, recording failure modes (misordering, omission, overconfidence) that threaten operational safety [10.1002/nem.2313]. Work in adjacent domains demonstrates that verifier‑assisted and retrieval‑augmented pipelines reduce factual errors and improve grounding, motivating similar guarded patterns for NetOps [10.36227/techrxiv.176784505.56675782/v1, 10.2139/ssrn.6608518]. Deterministic network verification techniques (e.g., header‑space analysis, specification checks) provide algorithmic foundations for validators able to statically check reachability and policy constraints without live execution [10.1145/3098822.3098834]. Surveys stressing auditability and oversight recommend generate→verify→repair architectures for safety‑critical operational contexts [10.6028/nist.ai.100-2e2023]. Our study sits at the intersection of these strands by executing a preregistered paired evaluation that measures first‑pass validity under an explicit validator+repair floor and archives all artifacts for reproducibility.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and hypotheses: We preregistered the study as cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1 prior to observing outcomes. Confirmatory hypotheses were: H1 — the guarded pipeline reduces first‑pass misconfiguration rate by ≥50% (relative) versus single‑shot generation; H2 — one or fewer automated repair iterations recover ≥75% of initially invalid configurations. The preregistration documented the planning assumption baseline pass rate = 0.40 used for power calculations; because this assumption materially affected the intended confirmatory test, we report it here explicitly.

Design and sampling semantics: We used a paired within‑task design with a frozen deterministic seed list of 300 tasks. For each seed the experiment produced a single shared LLM candidate (shared_initial_candidate semantics): that candidate served as the baseline response and as the starting point for the guarded arm's validation and possible repair. Planned episodes = 600 (two episodes per seed), initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1, maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1. The shared‑candidate pairing was preregistered to emulate operational workflows that remediate a single proposed plan; this choice increases within‑pair correlation and reduces the number of discordant pairs available for paired inference compared with independent‑draws designs, a tradeoff explicitly encoded in the preregistration's power arithmetic.

Model, sampling determinism, and provider policy: The declared generation model was gpt-5-mini. The recorded model configuration artifact shows temperature = null (execution/model_configuration.json; SHA-256: 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). Because the configuration recorded a null temperature, provider default sampling semantics are not specified in the archive; consequently sampling determinism is unspecified. We therefore treat generation stochasticity as an operational factor outside the confirmatory design rather than as a controlled variable. The preregistered call budget limited model calls to 600; the retry policy allowed a single retry for provider/infrastructure failures and the primary missingness treatment ('complete_pair_primary') drops pairs only when both calls in a pair failed.

Validator canonicalization, scoring, and repair: The frozen deterministic validator canonicalized outputs to a normalized AST and applied explicit workflow/dependency checks encoded in the task payloads. Success required satisfying the task's required_sequence and expected_final_state plus workflow policies (e.g., 'must_be_down_for_fields', 'final_group_constraints'). The repair adapter, invoked only when violations were reported on the shared candidate, was restricted to a single automated attempt per episode and aimed to minimally edit the candidate to remove reported violations. Repair prompts and responses were archived and revalidated by the same deterministic validator to produce the final guarded decision. All canonicalization, scoring rules, validator traces, repair prompts, and the analysis code were archived for reproducibility.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and artifact provenance: Planned episodes = 600; completed episodes = 600; complete pairs analyzed = 300. Model calls used = 301 (300 initial generations + 1 repair invocation). No provider or infrastructure failures occurred under the preregistered retry policy. All per‑task normalized responses, validator decisions, and repair traces are archived and constitute the authoritative source for the numeric counts reported below (see execution manifest and analysis artifacts).

Primary outcomes and inferential results: Baseline_success_count = 299/300 (99.667%); Guarded_success_count = 300/300 (100.0%). The archived paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; SHA-256: 3421adb52d5791a979397368165fc2062e6b9a4a771ce49c0bcac80b02215d55) records n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test on these counts yields p = 1.00. The observed absolute paired difference (guarded − baseline success rate) = 1/300 ≈ 0.0033333; the preregistered paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, bootstrap seed = 1729) is [0.00, 0.01]. The single allowed automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). These statistics and the bootstrap parameters are reproduced from the archived analysis artifacts (analysis_log.jsonl and condition_summary.csv).

Why McNemar p = 1.00 arose: the exact McNemar test conditions on the observed discordant total (n10 + n01 = 1 here). With only a single discordant pair the conditioned sampling distribution lacks the variability needed to reject the null for any small absolute effect; this numerical fact explains p = 1.00 despite the guarded arm correcting the lone failure. The paired bootstrap CI communicates the same limitation in interval form. The archived paired contingency artifact and bootstrap parameters are the authoritative record for this explanation.

Post‑hoc sensitivity bound tied to observed discordance: Given only one discordant pair, the maximum resolvable absolute paired improvement is 1/300 ≈ 0.00333. Thus the preregistered target (≥50% relative reduction from planned baseline 0.40, corresponding to an absolute +≈0.30) could not be detected with the observed data: achieving that absolute improvement at N=300 would require ≈90 net discordant pairs favoring guarded outputs. This arithmetic is artifact‑grounded in the archived contingency counts and the preregistered estimand definition.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation constrained by archived counts. The archived artifacts (paired contingency table, condition summary, and validator traces) directly constrain statistical conclusions: with near‑ceiling baseline prevalence (299/300), there is no practical headroom to detect large preregistered relative reductions. This outcome underlines the importance of aligning preregistered planning assumptions (baseline prevalence) with task‑bank difficulty and pairing semantics.

Methodological tradeoffs and operational framing. The shared_initial_candidate pairing models an operational workflow in which operators or automations remediate a single proposed plan; it increases ecological validity for remediation but reduces discordant counts for paired inference. An independent‑draws design addresses a different operational question and typically increases expected discordance for a given marginal success probability; selecting between these designs should be driven by the specific operational estimand and incorporated into power calculations.

Repair effectiveness as a conditional estimand. H2 (repair success conditional on initial failure) is a conditional probability defined on the initially invalid subset. The observed repair success (1/1) demonstrates feasibility but yields wide uncertainty (95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). When repair effectiveness is a primary claim, studies must ensure sufficient expected counts of initial failures by calibrating task difficulty or using adversarial augmentation so the conditional estimate is precise.

Construct validity and runtime semantics. Our validator performed deterministic static checks and canonicalization rather than live emulation. While static validators are valuable safety nets that avoid executing changes, they do not measure runtime dynamics such as control‑plane convergence or transient reachability. Claims about runtime consequences therefore require integrating emulation/simulation stages and preregistering how emulator outcomes map to success/failure. The execution manifest documents that our results are strictly conditional on the validator's static semantics.

Diagnostics and reproducibility. The validator traces recorded per episode (normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes, repair_applied) enabled precise failure taxonomy and repair auditing. The execution manifest records model_calls_used = 301 and repair_stage invocations = 1; paired contingency and bootstrap artifacts reproduce the inferential outputs. Maintaining such structured traces and archival primitives is necessary for explainable guardrails and reproducible post‑mortems in NetOps contexts.

Design recommendations grounded in artifacts. From the archived contingency and task difficulty fields, we recommend: (1) calibrate task difficulty or adversarially augment tasks to produce sufficient initial failures for intended estimands; (2) preregister pairing semantics and repair budgets and account for their impact on expected discordant counts in power calculations; (3) include emulation when runtime semantics matter and preregister how emulator outputs determine success/failure. Each recommendation is actionable from artifacts in the execution manifest (task generator difficulty knobs, validator violation codes, paired contingency counts).
sections.conclusion: We performed a preregistered paired experiment (N=300 pairs) comparing single‑shot LLM generation (gpt-5-mini) to a guarded pipeline consisting of a frozen deterministic validator and a single automated repair iteration. Baseline generation produced 299/300 valid outputs and the guarded pipeline produced 300/300 valid outputs; the single allowed automated repair corrected the lone invalid baseline output. The observed near‑ceiling baseline contradicted the preregistered planning assumption (baseline pass rate = 0.40) and removed the statistical headroom required to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction. Future confirmatory NetOps evaluations should (a) calibrate task difficulty or use adversarial augmentation to obtain a planned number of initial failures or discordant pairs, (b) preregister pairing semantics and repair budgets explicitly and fold them into power calculations, and (c) include emulation to measure runtime semantic effects when deployment claims require it. All raw outputs, validator traces, repair traces, the execution manifest, and analysis artifacts are archived and enumerated in the Disclosure Statement to permit reproduction of the reported counts and intervals.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and constrained vendor‑template scope limit external validity to broad production environments.
Single LLM (gpt-5-mini) and a single validator implementation restrict generality across model families and validator designs.

The preregistered power plan assumed a baseline pass rate = 0.40; the observed baseline (299/300) contradicted that assumption and removed headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction.
Sampling semantics (shared_initial_candidate) reused the same initial candidate across paired arms, increasing within‑pair correlation and reducing discordant pairs available to McNemar inference.

Validation used deterministic configuration/constraint checks rather than full dynamic emulation of runtime semantic effects; actual runtime consequences of configurations were not executed and remain unmeasured.

Model sampling determinism was not fixed: execution/model_configuration.json recorded temperature = null (SHA-256: 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa); provider default sampling behavior is unspecified in the archive, so generation stochasticity is an uncontrolled factor and may affect replicability under different provider defaults.

H2 repair‑success evidence is based on a single initially invalid case (1/1 → 100%), yielding a wide Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]; larger counts of initial failures are required to estimate repair effectiveness precisely.
